prompts: We search our server logs with Python regexes; {WS}/server.log shows what a log looks like. We need one regex that gives, for every log line containing an IPv4 address, the last date on that line (YYYY-MM-DD); lines without an address give nothing. Only real calendar dates count, with February allowed up to the 29th in every year. Addresses are dotted decimal, each part 0 to 255 with no leading zeros. A date or an address with a letter or digit right before or after it does not count. Save the regex alone in {WS}/regex.txt: we read the file, strip it, and run re.findall(pattern, log_text, re.MULTILINE) over a whole log, expecting exactly those dates in order.
answers:
**[goal]** One regex in `./regex.txt` that, via `re.findall(pattern, log_text, re.MULTILINE)`, returns the last valid `YYYY-MM-DD` on each line that contains an IPv4 address.

**[action]** Wrote the pattern as a single line-anchored expression: `^` + lookahead requiring a bounded IPv4 anywhere on the line, then lazy `.*?` to a bounded date, plus a negative lookahead rejecting any later date on the same line (so the captured date is the last one). IPv4 octets: `25[0-5]|2[0-4][0-9]|1[0-9][0-9]|[1-9][0-9]|[0-9]`, so 0-255 with no leading zeros. Dates split by month length: 31-day months, 30-day months, February `01-29`. Boundaries are `(?<![0-9A-Za-z])` / `(?![0-9A-Za-z])` on both token types. Verified with a 28-case script plus the real `server.log`.

**[result]** `regex.txt` holds the pattern only (no flags, no newline dependency). On `server.log` it returns `['2026-04-01', '2026-04-05', '2026-04-02']`: line 1 takes the later `build` date, line 2 (no address) and line 4 (`7781-20-4410`, invalid month, no address) yield nothing. Script output: `fails: 0` over all cases, including `256.1.1.1`, `01.1.1.1`, `1.1.1.01`, `v1.1.1.1`, `1.1.1.1x`, `x2026-12-31`, `2026-12-31x`, `2026-13-01`, `2026-04-31`, `2026-02-30`, `2026-02-29`, `2027-02-29`, and multi-date lines.

Assumptions where the brief is silent:
- "Letter or digit right before or after" is read literally, so a dot does not break a token: `from 1.1.1.1.` and `1.1.1.1.5` still count as containing an address. Excluding `.` would have broken normal sentence-final periods in logs.
- "Last date" means last *valid* date: `1.1.1.1 2026-04-30 then 2026-02-30` yields `2026-04-30`, since an impossible date is not a date.
- February 29 is accepted in every year, as stated, so `2027-02-29` counts.
- Address and date must be on the same line; the line-start anchor and `.` (no `DOTALL`) enforce that.
- Exactly one capture group, so `findall` returns the date strings only, in line order.

**[next]** Nothing open. If a future log uses `1.1.1.1.5`-style strings that must not count as addresses, add `.` to the address boundary classes.
